answer:
# BasicMed (US) — aircraft limits a pilot may operate under

## 0. The three answers, current as of the November 12, 2024 expansion

| # | Limit | Current value (on/after 12 Nov 2024) | Superseded value (2011 rule / 2017–11 Nov 2024) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Maximum takeoff weight (maximum certificated takeoff weight, MTOW) | **12,500 lb** | 6,000 lb |
| 2 | Number of occupants the aircraft may be **authorized to carry** | **7** | 6 |
| 3 | Number of **passengers on board** | **6** | 5 |

All three must be satisfied simultaneously; exceeding any one of them puts the flight outside BasicMed, and under 14 CFR 61.113(i) the limits apply to the *entire flight* (takeoff to touchdown), not just the portion the BasicMed pilot is manipulating the controls.

## 1. Authority chain (why these numbers and not the ones in the CFR print you may find)

1. **Origin.** BasicMed was created by §2307 of the FAA Extension, Safety, and Security Act of 2016 (PL 114-190), implemented by FAA as 14 CFR 61.113(i) plus 14 CFR part 68, effective 1 May 2017. Original limits: 6,000 lb MTOW / 6 occupants authorized / 5 passengers.
2. **Expansion.** §828 ("Expansion of BasicMed") of the FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024 (PL 118-63) directed the FAA to raise the ceilings to 12,500 lb / 7 occupants / 6 passengers, and to allow examiners (DPEs/SAEs) to conduct checks under BasicMed.
3. **FAA implementation.** FAA Notice **N 8000.386**, dated 11/14/24, states: "Per PL 118-63, Section 828, Expansion of BasicMed, the following aircraft limitations will apply **on or after November 12, 2024**: The aircraft is authorized to carry no more than seven occupants, the aircraft has an MTOW of no more than 12,500 pounds, and the aircraft is operated with no more than six passengers on board." The same notice recites the prior limits (six occupants / 6,000 lb / five passengers) as the pre-12 Nov 2024 standard.
4. **FAA public statement.** FAA newsroom, "FAA Updates BasicMed Program," Friday, November 15, 2024: "Increase the number of allowable passengers to six from five, and the number of occupants to seven from six. Increase the maximum aircraft takeoff weight to 12,500 lbs. from 6,000 lbs., **excluding transport category helicopters**. Allow pilot examiners to conduct flight checks using BasicMed..."
5. **FAA current guidance page.** faa.gov BasicMed page (fetched 2026-11-16): "Any aircraft authorized under federal law to carry not more than 7 occupants; Has a maximum certificated takeoff weight of not more than 12,500 pounds" and, under Operating Requirements, "Carries not more than six passengers."

**Publication-lag trap — read this before citing a CFR.** The govinfo PDF `CFR-2024-title14-vol2-sec61-113.pdf` still prints §61.113(i)(1) as "authorized to carry not more than 6 occupants, has a maximum takeoff weight of not more than 6,000 pounds, and is operated with no more than five passengers." That is the **1 January 2024 annual edition**, which by construction cannot contain a November 2024 amendment. It is correct only for flights before 12 November 2024. For any flight on/after 12 Nov 2024, cite the current eCFR text of §61.113(i)(1) (as amended) together with Notice N 8000.386. Do not quote the 2024 bound volume as "current."

## 2. How to apply each limit (definitions that decide real cases)

### 2.1 "Maximum takeoff weight" = maximum *certificated* takeoff weight
- Use the aircraft's **maximum certificated takeoff weight / maximum gross weight** from its design approval, not empty weight, not maximum landing weight, not a planned ramp weight.
- Type-certificated aircraft: read the **Type Certificate Data Sheet (TCDS)**, or the **STC/ATC** if the aircraft was altered. AC 68-1A expressly allows an aircraft type-certificated above the weight ceiling to be altered (STC/ATC) so that its *certificated* MTOW falls at or below the ceiling; once the design approval says so, it qualifies.
- Experimental/other special-airworthiness aircraft: the **FAA-issued operating limitations** establish the authorized MTOW (the FAA reviews weight-and-balance, including the operator-established maximum gross weight, before issuing the special airworthiness certificate).
- **Carve-out to watch:** the FAA's 15 Nov 2024 announcement attaches "excluding transport category helicopters" to the increase to 12,500 lb. The practical reading is that transport-category helicopters remain subject to the prior 6,000 lb ceiling. Confirm the exact amended regulatory wording in the current eCFR before relying on this in a specific operation.

### 2.2 "Authorized to carry not more than 7 occupants" = a certification/authorization count, not a seat count
- It is the number of occupants the aircraft is **authorized** to carry under its design approval (TC/STC/ATC) — or, for experimental aircraft, under its operating limitations — **including the pilot and any required flightcrew**.
- Installed seats are irrelevant. The FAA's own example: variants of the Piper PA-32 and PA-34 are *not* eligible under the pre-2024 rule because they are certificated for more than six occupants **even if only six seats are installed**. The reverse also matters: removing seats does not lower the authorized count; only a new design approval (STC/ATC) does.
- Determine it from the TCDS (passenger/occupant capacity or the seating configuration approved in the type design), not from the POH seating diagram alone.

### 2.3 "Not more than 6 passengers on board" = an operating count, crew excluded
- Occupants = everyone on board, **including the PIC**. Passengers = occupants other than the crew members required/acting for the flight.
- Consequence: with 7 authorized occupants and a 6-passenger cap, there must always be at least one crew member (the BasicMed PIC). The two limits bind at different points:
  - Single-pilot-certificated aircraft, 7 authorized occupants: PIC + up to 6 passengers. Passenger limit binds first.
  - Aircraft type-certificated for two pilots, 7 authorized occupants: PIC + second pilot + up to 5 passengers. Occupant limit binds first (7 total), and the passenger cap is not reached.
- A second pilot, a safety pilot, or a flight instructor on board occupies an occupant slot; whether they count as a "passenger" depends on whether they are acting as a required flightcrew member for that flight.
- This is an **operating** limit, so it is checked against the actual manifest for the actual flight, not against the aircraft's capacity.

### 2.4 Other BasicMed operating limits (context; not asked, but they travel with the three above)
At or below 18,000 ft MSL; indicated airspeed not exceeding 250 knots; within the United States (or another country in which BasicMed is authorized); not for compensation or hire; day or night, VFR or IFR.

## 3. Conformance check — illustrative aircraft (verify each against the current TCDS before use)

| Aircraft (illustrative) | Certificated MTOW | Authorized occupants | Result under current rule | Binding limit |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Cessna 172S | ~2,550 lb | 4 | Eligible | Passengers: PIC + 3 |
| Piper PA-32-301 | ~3,400 lb | 6 | Eligible | Passengers: PIC + 5 |
| Aircraft certificated 6,500 lb / 8 occupants (e.g., a light twin of that class) | ≤12,500 lb → weight OK | 8 → **fails** | Not eligible | Occupant authorization (8 > 7) |
| Cessna 208B-class turboprop single | ~8,750 lb → weight OK | typically >7 | Not eligible | Occupant authorization |
| Beech King Air 350-class | ~15,000 lb → **fails** | — | Not eligible | MTOW (15,000 > 12,500) |
| Same 6,500 lb / 8-occupant twin, **before 12 Nov 2024** | 6,500 > 6,000 → fails | 8 > 6 → fails | Not eligible | Both |

Note the third and fourth rows: the 2024 expansion moved the *weight* ceiling far above most light GA aircraft, so **occupant authorization is now the most common disqualifier** for high-performance singles and twins. That is the practical shift a pilot or dispatcher needs to internalize.

## 4. Procedure — qualifying a specific aircraft and flight

1. Identify the design approval: TC number, or STC/ATC if altered; for experimental, the special airworthiness certificate and its operating limitations.
2. Pull the TCDS (or STC/ATC, or operating limitations) and record (a) maximum certificated takeoff weight and (b) maximum authorized occupants.
3. Test 1: MTOW ≤ 12,500 lb (and, for a transport category helicopter, apply the FAA-stated exclusion and treat the ceiling as 6,000 lb pending confirmation of the amended text).
4. Test 2: authorized occupants ≤ 7, **including** required flightcrew.
5. Test 3: planned manifest has ≤ 6 passengers, and total souls ≤ 7, with the BasicMed pilot as PIC for the whole flight.
6. Test 4: the other operating limits (≤18,000 ft MSL, ≤250 KIAS, US or authorized country, no compensation or hire).
7. Record the TCDS/operating-limitation figures and the manifest in the flight records so the determination is auditable.

## 5. Common errors that produce a wrong answer

- **Quoting the 2024 bound CFR volume.** Gives 6,000/6/5. Superseded for flights on/after 12 Nov 2024.
- **Confusing seats with authorization.** A six-seat PA-32 variant certificated for seven occupants does not qualify on the seat count; conversely, pulling seats does not cure an over-capacity type certificate without an STC/ATC.
- **Treating the passenger cap as the occupant cap (or vice versa).** They are different numbers (6 vs 7) measuring different things; a two-pilot aircraft hits the occupant cap first.
- **Using empty weight, ramp weight, or max landing weight** instead of maximum certificated takeoff weight.
- **Assuming the 12,500 lb increase reaches transport category helicopters.** The FAA announcement excludes them.
- **Assuming the limits apply only while the BasicMed pilot is on the controls.** They apply to the whole flight.

## 6. Residual items to confirm (do not change the three answers)

1. Exact amended wording and effective-date treatment of the **transport category helicopter exclusion** in the current eCFR text of §61.113(i)(1).
2. Whether **14 CFR 91.319(j)** (experimental aircraft — AC 68-1A, 2017, states it prohibits carrying more than six occupants under BasicMed) was conformed to the seven-occupant standard by the 2024 expansion, or whether it still imposes a stricter six-occupant cap on experimental operations. Until confirmed against the current eCFR, treat experimental aircraft as capped at the lower of the two figures.
3. The codification vehicle for the expansion (direct final rule / conforming amendment) and the current eCFR revision date, for citation purposes.

## 7. One-line answer

Under BasicMed as expanded effective 12 November 2024, a pilot may operate an aircraft with a maximum certificated takeoff weight of **not more than 12,500 lb** (transport category helicopters excluded from the increase), that is **authorized to carry not more than 7 occupants** (including required flightcrew), and may carry **not more than 6 passengers on board**.

confirmations: The figures this answer gives for ask 1 stand in a passage found on its page.

answer:
US FEDERAL HOURS-OF-SERVICE LIMITS FOR DRIVERS OF PASSENGER-CARRYING COMMERCIAL MOTOR VEHICLES (MOTORCOACH)

1. BOTTOM LINE

Under 49 CFR 395.5 (interstate operation), a driver of a passenger-carrying CMV may not drive:

- Ask 1 — More than 10 hours of driving, measured from the end of the qualifying off-duty period. (10 hours)
- Ask 2 — The qualifying off-duty period that opens the driving window is 8 consecutive hours off duty. (8 hours)
- Ask 3 — For any period after having been on duty 15 hours, measured from the end of that same 8-consecutive-hour off-duty period. (15 hours)

These three operate simultaneously: the 8-hour off-duty period opens a 15-hour on-duty window, and inside that window no more than 10 of the hours may be driving. Driving must stop at whichever of the two caps is reached first.

2. REGULATORY BASIS — VERBATIM TEXT

49 CFR 395.5 (current eCFR, source note [70 FR 50073, Aug. 25, 2005]):

"§ 395.5 Maximum driving time for passenger-carrying vehicles.
Subject to the exceptions and exemptions in § 395.1:
(a) No motor carrier shall permit or require any driver used by it to drive a passenger-carrying commercial motor vehicle, nor shall any such driver drive a passenger-carrying commercial motor vehicle:
(1) More than 10 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty; or
(2) For any period after having been on duty 15 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty.
(b) No motor carrier shall permit or require a driver of a passenger-carrying commercial motor vehicle to drive, nor shall any driver drive a passenger-carrying commercial motor vehicle, regardless of the number of motor carriers using the driver's services, for any period after—
(1) Having been on duty 60 hours in any 7 consecutive days if the employing motor carrier does not operate commercial motor vehicles every day of the week; or
(2) Having been on duty 70 hours in any period of 8 consecutive days if the employing motor carrier operates commercial motor vehicles every day of the week."

The FMCSA 'Hours of Service for Motor Carriers of Passengers' guidance restates the same three figures: 10 hours driving following 8 consecutive hours off duty; no driving after 15 hours on duty following 8 consecutive hours off duty; and the 60-hour/7-day or 70-hour/8-day caps.

3. HOW THE THREE NUMBERS INTERACT — WORKED TIMELINE

Example A (pure driving day). Driver goes off duty at 22:00 and is released until 06:00 — 8 consecutive hours off duty, so the window opens at 06:00. The driver must stop driving no later than 16:00 (10 hours of driving) and in any event may not drive after 21:00 (15 hours on duty). Because 10 < 15, the driving cap binds first on a pure driving day.

Example B (mixed duty). Same 06:00 window start, but the driver spends 3 hours on duty not driving (loading, paperwork, passenger handling) before departing. Ten hours of driving then ends at 19:00 — the 13th hour of the window — even though the 15-hour on-duty limit would not be reached until 21:00. Total on duty at cessation: 13 hours. The 10-hour driving cap is the binding constraint.

Example C (long non-driving day). Same 06:00 window start, 6 hours on duty not driving first. Driving must stop at 19:00 (10 driving hours, 16th hour of the day)? No — driving is already prohibited after 21:00 by the 15-hour rule and, more restrictively here, only 9 of the remaining window hours are available before the 15-hour cap, so driving must stop at 21:00 at the latest, after at most 9 hours of driving. The 15-hour on-duty cap is the binding constraint.

Key corollaries:
- The 15-hour limit is a limit on DRIVING, not on being on duty. A driver may continue on-duty-not-driving work past the 15th hour; what is prohibited is driving after that point (subject to the 60/70-hour caps in §395.5(b)).
- The 8 hours must be consecutive and must be off duty. It need not be spent in a sleeper berth; ordinary off-duty time qualifies.
- The window restarts only when a new, complete 8-consecutive-hour off-duty period is taken.

4. QUALIFICATIONS AND CONDITIONS

(a) Scope assumed. This answer states the US FEDERAL interstate rule (49 CFR Part 395, FMCSA), which is the rule that applies to a for-hire or private motor carrier of passengers operating in interstate commerce. Purely INTRASTATE passenger operations may be governed by state hours-of-service rules that can differ from §395.5; a driver operating only within one state should be checked against that state's adoption of the federal limits (many states adopt them by reference, but this is not uniform). If the operation is intrastate, the three numbers above are the federal benchmark, not necessarily the controlling legal limit.

(b) Passenger vs. property rules. The passenger-carrier limits in §395.5 are a different rule set from the property-carrier limits in §395.3 (which use an 11-hour driving limit and a 14-hour on-duty window, plus a 30-minute break requirement). Do not apply the property-carrier numbers to a motorcoach. In particular, the 30-minute break requirement of §395.3(a)(3)(ii) is a property-carrying provision and is not part of §395.5.

(c) Exceptions in §395.1. Section 395.5 is expressly 'subject to the exceptions and exemptions in §395.1'. The ones most likely to matter for passenger carriers:
- §395.1(e) short-haul relief: a driver operating within a 150 air-mile radius of the normal work reporting location and released from duty within 14 consecutive hours is exempt from the record-of-duty-status requirement. This is a LOGGING exemption only — it does not enlarge the 10-hour driving limit or the 15-hour on-duty limit. (Note 14 hours < 15 hours, so the release condition is tighter than the on-duty cap.)
- §395.1(g)(3) sleeper berth (passenger carriers): a driver of a passenger-carrying CMV equipped with a sleeper berth may accumulate the equivalent of 8 consecutive hours off duty by taking two rest periods in the sleeper berth, provided the four requirements of §395.1(g)(3)(i)–(iv) are met. Operationally, the effect is that the two paired periods together satisfy the off-duty prerequisite and the 10- and 15-hour limits are recalculated from the end of the first period of the pair rather than requiring one unbroken 8-hour block. Because the sub-conditions are paragraph-specific and have been amended over time, verify the current text of §395.1(g)(3)(i)–(iv) before relying on a split.
- §395.1(j) travel time ('cushioning') and relief-driver travel: travel at the carrier's direction but not driving is on-duty time unless the driver is afforded at least 8 consecutive hours off duty on arrival, in which case the travel period may be treated as off duty. This affects whether the 8-hour reset is satisfied and how the 15-hour window is counted.
- Other §395.1 exceptions (e.g., transportation of school children, certain government-operated vehicles under §390.3(f), and emergency relief under §390.23) can remove or suspend the limits for defined operations. Whether any applies is a fact question about the specific operation and must be confirmed before relying on it.
- Adverse driving conditions under §395.1(b) can permit a limited amount of additional driving time (on the order of 2 hours) in defined circumstances the driver did not know about before dispatch. It is an exception to be verified against the current paragraph text, it does not extend the 60/70-hour caps, and it is not part of the base answer above.

(d) Multi-day caps (context, not asked). Section 395.5(b) independently bars driving after 60 hours on duty in any 7 consecutive days (carrier not operating CMVs every day of the week) or 70 hours on duty in any 8 consecutive days (carrier operating every day). These accumulate across days and can shut a driver down before the daily 10- or 15-hour caps are reached. Section 395.5 contains no 34-hour restart provision of the kind found for property carriers in §395.3(c); the 60/70-hour limits are computed on a rolling 7- or 8-consecutive-day basis, so hours age out as the window rolls forward. Confirm the treatment of any restart under the carrier's applicable rule set and any state rule before building a schedule around it.

(e) On-duty definition. 'On-duty time' runs from when the driver begins work or is required to be ready for work until relieved of work and all responsibility. Compensated work for a non-motor-carrier employer also counts as on-duty time, and a multiple-employer driver must furnish a signed statement of total on-duty time for the preceding 7 days (§395.8(j)). All such time counts against the 15-hour window and the 60/70-hour caps.

(f) Recordkeeping. Drivers subject to §395.5 must keep a record of duty status under §395.8 and, in most cases, use an ELD; the ELD rules apply to most motor carriers of passengers, including drivers domiciled in Canada or Mexico operating in the US. Non-business private motor carriers of passengers are not subject to the Part 395 recordkeeping requirements. Drivers required to prepare a record of duty status no more than 8 days in any 30-day period are excepted from the ELD rule.

5. ENFORCEMENT CONTEXT

Driving beyond the 10-hour limit or after the 15-hour on-duty limit is an hours-of-service violation; a driver may be declared out of service under §395.13 and the carrier is exposed to civil penalties under Part 386. The practical compliance test at roadside is the duty-status record: the officer reconstructs the end of the last qualifying 8-consecutive-hour off-duty period and measures both the driving time and the on-duty time from that point.

6. VERIFICATION AND EFFECTIVE DATE

Figures taken from the current eCFR text of 49 CFR 395.5 and FMCSA's 'Hours of Service for Motor Carriers of Passengers' publication (2022), both retrieved 2026-11-16. Section 395.5 has been stable in this form since 70 FR 50073 (Aug. 25, 2005); the surrounding Part 395 text carries later amendments (78 FR 58485; 78 FR 64181; 84 FR 48081; 85 FR 33452). Confirm the current text and any recent rulemaking before relying on these numbers for a compliance program, and confirm which §395.1 exceptions apply to the specific operation.

question: M5
answer:
REST REQUIREMENTS FOR PART 135 FLIGHT ATTENDANTS AFTER A SCHEDULED DUTY PERIOD OF 14 HOURS OR LESS

1. ANSWER

   (a) Base requirement: at least 9 consecutive hours of scheduled rest.
   (b) Reducible to: 8 consecutive hours, but only if the certificate holder also gives the flight attendant a subsequent rest period of at least 10 consecutive hours that is scheduled to begin no later than 24 hours after the beginning of the reduced rest period.

   Governing provision: 14 CFR 135.273(b)(2) and (b)(3).

2. CONTROLLING TEXT (14 CFR 135.273, current eCFR and 2025 CFR print)

   135.273(b)(1): "Except as provided in paragraphs (b)(4), (b)(5), and (b)(6) of this section, no certificate holder may assign a flight attendant to a scheduled duty period of more than 14 hours."

   135.273(b)(2): "Except as provided in paragraph (b)(3) of this section, a flight attendant scheduled to a duty period of 14 hours or less as provided under paragraph (b)(1) of this section must be given a scheduled rest period of at least 9 consecutive hours. This rest period must occur between the completion of the scheduled duty period and the commencement of the subsequent duty period."

   135.273(b)(3): "The rest period required under paragraph (b)(2) of this section may be scheduled or reduced to 8 consecutive hours if the flight attendant is provided a subsequent rest period of at least 10 consecutive hours; this subsequent rest period must be scheduled to begin no later than 24 hours after the beginning of the reduced rest period and must occur between the completion of the scheduled duty period and the commencement of the subsequent duty period."

   135.273(b)(10): "No certificate holder may assign a flight attendant any duty period with the certificate holder unless the flight attendant has had at least the minimum rest required under this section."

   135.273(b)(11): "No certificate holder may assign a flight attendant to perform any duty with the certificate holder during any required rest period."

   Applicability: 135.261(e) — "Section 135.273 prescribes duty period limitations and rest requirements for flight attendants in all operations conducted under this part." The rule therefore reaches on-demand (unscheduled) Part 135 charter operations, not only scheduled passenger operations. It is keyed to flight attendants actually used in the certificate holder's operation; the operator's ops specs and the aircraft's type-certificate/configuration determine whether a flight attendant must be carried, but once one is used, 135.273 governs that person's duty and rest.

3. DEFINITION THAT DRIVES COMPLIANCE

   135.273(a): "Rest period means the period free of all responsibility for work or duty should the occasion arise."

   Consequences the operator must build into its schedule:
   - The whole interval between completion of the scheduled duty period and commencement of the subsequent duty period must be rest. The 9 (or 8) hours is not a block of free time somewhere inside that interval; the interval itself must be at least that long.
   - Any duty, positioning assignment, administrative task, training, or required response obligation during the interval defeats the rest period and violates (b)(11).
   - Whether on-call/reserve time qualifies as rest turns on whether the flight attendant is in fact free of all responsibility and not required to respond. Where a reserve obligation requires response, crediting it as rest is not defensible under the quoted definition; it should be excluded from the rest computation.

4. HOW THE REDUCTION WORKS — ALL CONDITIONS MUST BE MET

   To use the 8-hour figure, the certificate holder must satisfy every one of the following:
   (1) The preceding scheduled duty period was 14 hours or less (so (b)(2)/(b)(3), not (b)(7)-(b)(9), is the operative paragraph).
   (2) The reduced rest is at least 8 consecutive hours, scheduled in advance as such.
   (3) A subsequent rest period of at least 10 consecutive hours is provided.
   (4) That subsequent rest is scheduled to begin no later than 24 hours after the beginning of the reduced rest period (i.e., no later than 24 hours after the start of the reduced rest, which is the moment the prior duty period completed).
   (5) That subsequent rest occurs between completion of the scheduled duty period and commencement of the subsequent duty period — it is the rest following the next duty period, not an extra block inserted into the reduced rest itself.
   (6) The flight attendant actually receives the minimum rest; (b)(10) bars assignment otherwise, so a scheduled-but-not-realized rest is a violation.

   The reduction is elective and must be affirmatively scheduled. If the operator does not schedule the 10-hour subsequent rest, the default 9-hour requirement applies and an 8-hour rest is a violation.

5. WORKED TIMELINE

   Assume the scheduled duty period completes at 2200 local.

   Base case (9 hours): rest 2200-0700. No duty may be assigned to the flight attendant before 0700.

   Reduced case (8 hours): rest 2200-0600; next duty may commence at 0600. Because the subsequent rest of at least 10 consecutive hours must begin no later than 2200 the following day (24 hours after the 2200 start of the reduced rest), the duty period commencing at 0600 must be scheduled to complete no later than 2200 so the 10-hour subsequent rest can begin inside the window. In practice the 14-hour scheduled duty cap in (b)(1) is the tighter limit: a 0600-2000 duty period completes at 2000, the 10-hour subsequent rest runs 2000-0600 the next morning, and the next duty may commence at 0600. The 24-hour condition is what constrains the operator when the post-reduction duty period is itself long or is delayed; if the following duty would run past the 24-hour point, the 8-hour reduction cannot lawfully be used for that pairing and the 9-hour rest must be given.

6. WHAT IS NOT A LAWFUL ROUTE TO LESS REST

   - No reduction below 8 consecutive hours for any reason under (b)(2)/(b)(3).
   - Section 135.273 contains no unforeseen-circumstances / circumstances-beyond-control rest-escalation clause for flight attendants comparable to 135.267(e). Delays, weather, or maintenance do not create an affirmative rest entitlement under 135.273, but neither do they permit rest below the 8-hour floor; the minimums in (b)(2)/(b)(3) and the assignment bars in (b)(10) and (b)(11) still apply.
   - The flight-crewmember numbers in 135.267 (10 consecutive hours of rest during the 24 hours preceding planned completion; the 11/12/16-hour escalations in 135.267(e)) do not apply to a flight attendant unless the operator makes the 135.273(c) election described in paragraph 8 below.
   - There is no provision to credit deadhead, ground positioning, or reduced-duty time against the rest minimum. Rest is rest.
   - The 135.273(b)(9) cap (no duty period over 14 hours in the 24 hours commencing after the start of a reduced rest) is written "[n]otwithstanding paragraphs (b)(4), (b)(5), and (b)(6)" and applies to the 10-hour reduction under (b)(8). By its terms it does not attach to the 8-hour reduction under (b)(3); the operator should not assume it does, and equally should not assume it can be ignored where a (b)(8) reduction is in play.

7. IF THE DUTY PERIOD IS MORE THAN 14 HOURS (SEPARATE BRANCH — DO NOT CONFUSE WITH THE ANSWER ABOVE)

   For completeness, because the two branches are frequently conflated: a flight attendant scheduled to a duty period of more than 14 hours (lawful only under (b)(4)-(b)(6), which require additional flight attendants on the flights) must receive a scheduled rest of at least 12 consecutive hours under (b)(7). That 12-hour rest may be scheduled or reduced to 10 consecutive hours under (b)(8) if a subsequent rest of at least 14 consecutive hours is provided that begins no later than 24 hours after the beginning of the reduced rest. If the (b)(8) reduction is used, (b)(9) forbids scheduling that flight attendant for a duty period of more than 14 hours during the 24-hour period commencing after the beginning of the reduced rest. These figures (12 / 10 / 14) apply only to the over-14-hour scheduled duty case and must not be substituted into the 14-hours-or-less answer.

   Note the structural point: 135.273 keys the rest requirement to the SCHEDULED duty period. An actual overrun of a duty period that was scheduled at 14 hours or less does not, on the face of the quoted text, convert the case into a (b)(7) 12-hour-rest case. The 9-hour (or properly reduced 8-hour) minimum still applies, and the operator should treat any overrun as a scheduling/fatigue-review trigger under its manual and SMS rather than as a self-executing change to the rest figure.

8. THE ONE PATH THAT CHANGES THE ANSWER: 135.273(c) ELECTION

   135.273(c): "Notwithstanding paragraph (b) of this section, a certificate holder may apply the flight crewmember flight time and duty limitations and rest requirements of this part to flight attendants for all operations conducted under this part provided that— (1) The certificate holder establishes written procedures that— (i) Apply to all flight attendants used in the certificate holder's operation; (ii) Include the flight crewmember requirements contained in subpart F of this part, as appropriate to the operation being conducted, except that rest facilities on board the aircraft are not required; and (iii) Include provisions to add one flight attendant to the minimum flight attendant complement for each flight crewmember who is in excess of the minimum number required in the aircraft type certificate data sheet and who is assigned to the aircraft under the provisions of subpart F of this part, as applicable. (iv) Are approved by the Administrator and described or referenced in the certificate holder's operations specifications..."

   If, and only if, the operator has such approved written procedures referenced in its ops specs, the flight-attendant rest question is answered by the flight-crewmember rules instead — for an unscheduled one- or two-pilot crew that means 135.267(d) (at least 10 consecutive hours of rest during the 24-hour period preceding the planned completion time of the assignment) and, where applicable, 135.267(c)(1) and (e). Absent that election — which is the default assumption for an on-demand charter operator unless its ops specs say otherwise — the 9/8-hour answer in paragraph 1 controls. The election is all-or-nothing for all flight attendants used in the operation; it cannot be applied selectively to gain a shorter rest on one pairing.

9. OPERATOR COMPLIANCE PROCEDURE

- RFC 8740 — the companion document that defined use of TLS 1.3 with HTTP/2; RFC 9113 folds that content into the main specification and therefore obsoletes it as a separate document (see Appendix B of RFC 9113, quoted in §2).

## 2. Evidence (primary sources, quoted)

From the RFC Editor's rendering of RFC 9113 (`https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9113.html`), header block:

> Obsoletes: 7540, 8740

> This specification describes an optimized expression of the semantics of the Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP), referred to as HTTP version 2 (HTTP/2). ... This document obsoletes RFCs 7540 and 8740.

Three independent metadata paths (RFC header field, abstract prose, Datatracker record) agree on the same pair, so the answer does not rest on a single field.

3. **Obsoletes ≠ Updates.** A document that *updates* HTTP/2 adds to or amends the specification without replacing it, and would not appear in the `Obsoletes` field. # UK statutory minimum wage rates effective 1 April 2026

## 1. Direct answers

| # | Question | Rate from 1 April 2026 |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | National Living Wage — workers aged 21 and over | **£12.71 per hour** |
| 2 | National Minimum Wage — 18 to 20 Year Old Rate | **£10.85 per hour** |

Both are gross hourly rates in pounds sterling, quoted to the penny, applying across England, Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland.

## 2. Full April 2026 rate table (for payroll set-up)

| Band | Rate from 1 Apr 2026 | Rate to 31 Mar 2026 | Increase (£) | Increase (%) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| National Living Wage (21 and over) | £12.71 | £12.21 | £0.50 | 4.1% |
| 18-20 Year Old Rate | £10.85 | £10.00 | £0.85 | 8.5% |
| 16-17 Year Old Rate | £8.00 | £7.55 | £0.45 | 6.0% |
| Apprentice Rate | £8.00 | £7.55 | £0.45 | 6.0% |
| Accommodation Offset (per day) | £11.10 | £10.66 | £0.44 | 4.1% |

The two requested rates are rows 1 and 2. Rows 3–5 are supplied because they are needed to complete a payroll rate table and because the 18–20 rate cannot be applied correctly without the age-threshold rules below.

## 3. Legal basis and confirmation status

- **Operative instrument:** The National Minimum Wage (Amendment) Regulations 2026, SI 2026/357. Made 19 March 2026; came into force 1 April 2026; extends to England and Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland.
  - Reg. 2(2): in reg. 4 of the 2015 Regulations (the national living wage), for "£12.21" substitute **"£12.71"**.
  - Reg. 2(3)(a): in reg. 4A(1)(b) (workers aged 18 or over but not yet 21), for "£10.00" substitute **"£10.85"**.
  - Reg. 2(3)(b)–(c): 16-17 and apprentice rates to £8.00; reg. 2(4): accommodation offset to £11.10 per day.
- **Recommendation and acceptance trail:** Low Pay Commission recommendations submitted 27 October 2025; Government accepted them in full at the Autumn Budget on 26 November 2025; LPC advice published 26 November 2025; GOV.UK rate pages and the LPC press release of 1 April 2026 restate the same figures.
- **Status:** These are **in-force statutory rates, not forecasts or projections**. No estimate, interpolation or rounding has been applied by me; the figures are lifted verbatim from the regulations and the GOV.UK rate tables.

## 4. Threshold and consistency checks performed

- 12.71 − 12.21 = 0.50 → matches the published £0.50 increase; 0.50 ÷ 12.21 = 4.09% → matches the published 4.1%.
- 10.85 − 10.00 = 0.85 → matches the published £0.85 increase; 0.85 ÷ 10.00 = 8.5% exactly → matches the published 8.5%.
- 8.00 − 7.55 = 0.45 → matches the published £0.45 increase; 0.45 ÷ 7.55 = 5.96% → matches the published 6.0%.
- 11.10 − 10.66 = 0.44 → matches the published £0.44; 0.44 ÷ 10.66 = 4.13% → matches the published 4.1%.
- LPC states the 18-20 rate is now 85% of the NLW: 12.71 × 0.85 = 10.8035, consistent with £10.85 after rounding up to the penny. The two requested values are therefore mutually consistent, not merely co-published.
- The legal instrument and the GOV.UK tables agree figure-for-figure; there is no conflict to resolve.

## 5. Age-band application rules (the practical trap)

- The National Living Wage applies to workers **aged 21 and over**. Workers aged 20 and under are on the National Minimum Wage age bands regardless of length of service.
- The NLW age threshold history matters if you are back-computing arrears: 25+ before 1 April 2021, 23+ from April 2021, 21+ from 1 April 2024. Do not apply the 21+ threshold to periods before 1 April 2024.
- Age is taken at the worker's birthday, not the pay period start — a worker turning 21 mid-period moves to £12.71 from the start of the pay reference period in which the birthday falls (or the first day of the pay reference period following, depending on the pay reference period rules applied to the employer's pay cycle). Confirm against the 2015 Regulations for the specific pay reference period in use.
- **Apprentices:** entitled to the £8.00 apprentice rate if aged under 19, or aged 19+ and in the first year of their apprenticeship. Once aged 19+ **and** past the first year, they move to the full rate for their age — e.g. an apprentice aged 21 who has completed year one is entitled to £12.71, not £8.00.
- **Accommodation offset:** £11.10 per day is the maximum an employer may deduct (or count as paid) for providing living accommodation; it is a daily figure, not hourly, and the £12.71/£10.85 rates are before that offset is applied.

## 6. Common confusion to avoid when this figure is circulated

There are two different "living wage" numbers in UK use:

- **National Living Wage (statutory) = £12.71 from April 2026** — set by regulations, enforced by HMRC, applies to all employers. **This is the figure answering ask 1.**
- **Real Living Wage (voluntary) = set separately by the Living Wage Foundation**, higher than the statutory rate and updated on a different cycle (announced in the autumn, effective usually 1 April for the UK rate). It is not law and has no statutory enforcement.

If a colleague or downstream system quotes a higher figure and calls it "the living wage", they are almost certainly quoting the Living Wage Foundation rate. Ask 1 must be answered with £12.71.

1. Open https://www.gov.uk/national-minimum-wage-rates and read the row headed **April 2026** — columns 21 and over, 18 to 20, Under 18, Apprentice.
2. Cross-check against https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2026/357/made — reg. 2(2) should read £12.71 and reg. 2(3)(a) should read £10.85.
3. Confirm the effective date is **1 April 2026**, not the announcement date (26 November 2025) and not the making date (19 March 2026). Rates change on 1 April every year.
4. Confirm the figures are to the penny in GBP and are gross hourly pay.

## 8. Downstream payroll actions this implies

- Update the payroll rate table effective 1 April 2026: NLW £12.71, 18-20 £10.85, 16-17 £8.00, apprentice £8.00, accommodation offset £11.10/day.
- Re-run a minimum-wage compliance sweep across all hourly-paid and salaried-hours workers, checking each worker against the band for their age at the relevant date.
- Re-check salary sacrifice arrangements, deductions for uniforms/tools, and unpaid working time — these are the usual causes of effective pay falling below the statutory rate even where the headline rate is set correctly.
- Retain NMW records for at least six years (three years is the statutory minimum for most pay records; six is the HMRC enforcement expectation).

SHORT-HAUL EXCEPTION (49 CFR 395.1(e)(1)) — THE TWO REQUESTED FIGURES

ANSWER 1 — RADIUS: 150 air miles.
The driver must operate within a 150 air-mile radius of the normal work reporting location. The regulation states this as '150 air-mile radius (172.6 statute miles).' The 172.6 figure is the section's own arithmetic conversion of 150 air miles; the governing unit is AIR MILES, and the radius is measured as a straight-line (great-circle) distance from the normal work reporting location, not as road miles and not as a statute-mile driving distance. Driving 150 road miles from the terminal does not by itself satisfy or violate the test — the test is the air-mile radius.

ANSWER 2 — RELEASE: 14 consecutive hours.
The driver must return to the work reporting location and be released from work within 14 consecutive hours. The 14 hours run from the time the driver comes on duty; it is a single continuous clock, and off-duty time taken inside that window does not extend it. (The one carve-out in the text is the driver-salesperson, who is excused from the return-and-release requirement of (e)(1)(ii) but is still bound by the 150 air-mile radius in (e)(1)(i).)

VERBATIM GOVERNING TEXT — 49 CFR 395.1(e)(1) (eCFR current; identical in the 2024 and 2025 GovInfo annual editions of 49 CFR vol. 5):

"(e) Short-haul operations —
(1) 150 air-mile radius driver. A driver is exempt from the requirements of §§ 395.8 and 395.11 if:
(i) The driver operates within a 150 air-mile radius (172.6 statute miles) of the normal work reporting location;
(ii) The driver, except a driver-salesperson, returns to the work reporting location and is released from work within 14 consecutive hours;
(iii)(A) A property-carrying commercial motor vehicle driver has at least 10 consecutive hours off-duty separating each 14 hours on-duty;
(B) A passenger-carrying commercial motor vehicle driver has at least 8 consecutive hours off-duty separating each 14 hours on-duty; and
(iv) The motor carrier that employs the driver maintains and retains for a period of 6 months accurate and true time records showing:
(A) The time the driver reports for duty each day;
(B) The total number of hours the driver is on-duty each day;
(C) The time the driver is released from duty each day; and
(D) The total time for the preceding 7 days in accordance with § 395.8(j)(2) for drivers used for the first time or intermittently."

SUMMARY TABLE
| Element | Value | Citation |
|---|---|---|
| Radius from normal work reporting location | 150 air miles (= 172.6 statute miles straight-line) | 395.1(e)(1)(i) |
| Return to work reporting location and release from work | within 14 consecutive hours | 395.1(e)(1)(ii) |
| Minimum off-duty separating each 14 hours on-duty | 10 consecutive hours (property-carrying CMV); 8 (passenger-carrying) | 395.1(e)(1)(iii) |
| Carrier time-record retention | 6 months | 395.1(e)(1)(iv) |
| Records excused | RODS under 395.8 and ELD-related 395.11 | 395.1(e)(1) opening clause |

WHAT THE EXEMPTION ACTUALLY RELIEVES
A driver meeting every condition of 395.1(e)(1) is exempt from 395.8 (records of duty status) and 395.11 (the supporting-documents/ELD-related requirement cross-referenced there). The exemption is conditional and cumulative: miss any one of (i)-(iv) on a given day and the exemption does not apply for that day, and the driver must complete RODS (paper or ELD) for that day. The radius and the 14-hour release are conditions (i) and (ii); they are not standalone safe harbors.

MEASUREMENT AND COMPLIANCE NOTES (the practical failure modes)
1. Air miles, not road miles. Compute the straight-line distance from the normal work reporting location to the farthest point the vehicle reaches during the duty tour. A route whose road distance is 180 miles can still be inside a 150 air-mile radius; a route with 140 road miles can leave the radius if it zig-zags outward.
2. The radius attaches to the 'normal work reporting location' — the fixed location the driver reports to and is released from — not to the driver's home, not to the shipper, and not to wherever the day happens to start.
3. The 14 hours is measured from coming on duty to release from work at the work reporting location. It is not 14 hours of driving, and it is not extended by off-duty time inside the window, by a 30-minute break, or by the adverse-driving-conditions 2-hour extension (that extension modifies 395.3 driving limits, not the (e)(1)(ii) release condition).
4. The driver must both RETURN to the location and BE RELEASED there within the 14 hours; returning at hour 13 and continuing to work until hour 15 fails the condition.
5. Time records are mandatory even though RODS are not: the carrier must keep 6 months of report-for-duty time, total on-duty hours, release-from-duty time, and the preceding 7 days' total hours for new/intermittent drivers.
6. Drivers who fall outside the exception on any day must log that day; the carrier should have a documented check (radius calculation from the reporting location plus a daily 14-hour release check) rather than relying on the driver's judgment.

FIGURES THAT ARE *NOT* THE ANSWER (disambiguation, so the numbers are not confused downstream)
- 100 air miles / 12 hours: the pre-2020 short-haul figures. FMCSA's HOS Final Rule lengthened the maximum on-duty period from 12 to 14 hours and the radius from 100 to 150 air miles. Do not use 100/12.
- 100 air miles in 395.1(p): the separate motion-picture-production-site exemption from 395.3(a). Different exemption, different figure — not the short-haul RODS exception.
- 395.1(e)(2) (property-carrying CMV not requiring a CDL): also uses a 150 air-mile radius, but its time conditions are 'not driving after the 14th hour on 5 days of any 7' and 'after the 16th hour on 2 days of any 7,' with return to the location at the end of each duty tour. The 16-hour figure belongs to that provision, not to the release condition asked about here.
- 11-hour driving limit, 60/70-hour limits, 30-minute break: separate 395.3 requirements; the short-haul driver under (e)(1) is relieved of RODS and of the 30-minute break, but the question asked only for the radius and the release window.

VERSION CONTROL
Values verified against 49 CFR 395.1(e)(1) as published on eCFR (current) and in the 2024 and 2025 GovInfo annual CFR editions; the three sources are textually identical on both figures. Both figures are stable as of the 2020 HOS amendments. Any future amendment to 395.1(e)(1) would supersede this answer; the citation, not a secondary summary, controls.

# Minimum rest between duty periods for a US airline flight attendant

## Answer

**10 consecutive hours.** For a US air carrier operating under 14 CFR Part 121 (domestic, flag, or supplemental operations), a flight attendant scheduled to a duty period of 14 hours or less must be given a scheduled rest period of **at least 10 consecutive hours**, and that rest period **may not be reduced below 10 consecutive hours under any circumstances**. The rest must fall between the completion of the scheduled duty period and the commencement of the subsequent duty period.

Source: 14 CFR 121.467(b)(2)–(3), as amended by the FAA final rule *Flight Attendant Duty Period Limitations and Rest Requirements* (FAARA 2018 §335(a)), and as printed in the current codified text (CFR 2025 title 14 vol. 3, §121.467).

## The complete rest table (§121.467)

| Situation | Required scheduled rest | Reducible? | Cite |
|---|---|---|---|
| Scheduled duty period of 14 hours or less | **10 consecutive hours** | **No** — may not be reduced below 10 | 121.467(b)(1)–(3) |
| Scheduled duty period of more than 14 hours but not more than 20 hours (only as permitted by the augmented-crew provisions (b)(4)–(b)(6)) | **12 consecutive hours** | Yes, to 10 consecutive hours, **only if** a subsequent rest period of at least 14 consecutive hours is scheduled to begin no later than 24 hours after the beginning of the reduced rest | 121.467(b)(7)–(8) |
| Any 7 consecutive calendar days | At least **24 consecutive hours** relieved from all further duty (additional to, not a substitute for, the between-duty-period rest above) | No | 121.467(b)(13) |

So the answer to "how much rest between duty days" is **10 hours as the floor in every case**, rising to **12 hours** whenever the preceding duty period was extended past 14 hours under the augmentation provisions. A carrier that schedules 10 hours after a 15-hour duty period is out of compliance unless it fits the (b)(8) reduced-rest/makeup-rest pattern.

## What counts as the rest period

- **Definition.** "Rest period" means the period free of all restraint or duty for a certificate holder conducting domestic, flag, or supplemental operations and free of all responsibility for work or duty should the occasion arise. (§121.467(a).)
- **No duty during rest.** The carrier may not assign a flight attendant to perform any duty with the certificate holder during any required rest period. (§121.467(b)(11).)
- **Transportation is not rest.** Time spent in transportation, not local in character, that the carrier requires and provides to move a flight attendant to an airport to serve on a flight, or home from an airport where the flight attendant was relieved, is **not** part of a rest period. (§121.467(b)(12).) Practically: a 05:00 hotel-van departure does not eat into the 10 hours; the 10 hours must be complete before the transportation begins.
- **The clock runs from actual release, not scheduled release.** The rest period is measured from completion of the duty period to commencement of the next. The relief-from-excess-duty provision in (b)(14) protects the carrier from being deemed to have *scheduled* an over-limit duty when weather or similar circumstances beyond its control stretch the flights — it does **not** shorten the rest that must follow the duty period as actually flown. If a 13-hour scheduled duty runs to 15 hours, the rest obligation follows the actual duty, and the >14-hour rest provisions must be re-checked.
- **"Duty day" is not a defined term.** Part 121 speaks of the "duty period," and the rest requirement is expressed between duty periods, not between calendar days. A duty period that crosses midnight does not reset anything; the 10 hours run from release.

## Worked scheduling checks

1. **Baseline.** Duty period ends 21:00. Earliest permissible report for the next duty period: **07:00** the following day (10 consecutive hours).
2. **Extended duty, full rest.** Duty period 06:00–20:30 (14 h 30 min). Because it exceeds 14 hours, 12 consecutive hours of rest are required: earliest report **08:30** the next day.
3. **Extended duty, reduced rest with makeup.** Same duty ending 20:30. The carrier may reduce to 10 hours (report 06:30 the next day) **only if** it schedules a subsequent rest of at least 14 consecutive hours beginning no later than 20:30 the following day — i.e., the next duty period must end by 20:30 and be followed by rest until no earlier than 10:30 the day after. If that makeup rest cannot be guaranteed, the 12-hour rest must be given.
4. **Delay case.** Duty scheduled 08:00–20:00 but actually released at 22:15 due to a diversion. Rest runs from 22:15; earliest report 08:15 the next day. Do not plan against the scheduled release time.

## Scope and assumptions the answer rests on

1. **Part 121 scheduled carrier.** This is the "US airline" case. If the operation is actually a commuter or on-demand operator under **Part 135**, the figure is different and lower: §135.273(b)(2)–(3) requires 9 consecutive hours, reducible to 8 with a subsequent ≥10-hour rest beginning no later than 24 hours after the reduced rest began; and §135.273(b)(7)–(8) requires 12 hours for duty periods over 14 hours, reducible to 10 with a ≥14-hour makeup rest. **Confirm the operating certificate and operations specifications before using this memo for a 135 operator.**
2. **Regulatory floor, not contract.** Collective bargaining agreements and company policies routinely exceed 10 hours (12-hour layover minimums are common). This memo states the legal minimum; a CBA or manual provision that is more generous controls the individual flight attendant's entitlement and should be checked separately. A CBA can never lawfully go below the regulatory floor.
3. **Flight attendants, not pilots.** Pilot rest is governed by different provisions (Part 117 for Part 121, Part 135 Subpart F for 135). Do not transfer this figure to a flightcrew member.
4. **Part 117 election.** Under §121.467(c), a certificate holder may elect to apply the Part 117 flightcrew flight-time/duty/rest requirements to flight attendants, provided it establishes written procedures meeting the stated conditions. If a carrier has made that election, the governing rest provision is Part 117, not (b)(2), and the analysis must be re-run against §117.25. I have not verified §117.25's text here and deliberately do not state a figure for that path.
5. **State and foreign law.** State law cannot authorize less than the FAA minimum for a covered carrier; foreign jurisdictions may impose additional local requirements on the ground. Neither lowers the 10-hour floor.

## Superseded guidance — do not cite

The FAA's public FAQ page still displays the **pre-amendment** figures (9 consecutive hours, reducible to 8). That text reflects §121.467(b)(2)–(3) as it read before the FAARA 2018 §335(a) amendments. The current codified rule is 10 consecutive hours with **no reduction permitted**. Any compliance document, crew-scheduling rule, or training material that still states 9/8 for Part 121 is out of date and should be corrected; the FAA's own final rule explicitly states the minimum "will increase from at least 9 consecutive hours to at least 10 consecutive hours" and that the reduction authority is removed.

## Verification checklist for a compliance review

- [ ] Operating certificate confirmed as Part 121 domestic/flag/supplemental.
- [ ] No §121.467(c) Part 117 election in the carrier's written procedures (or, if elected, the analysis re-run against Part 117).
- [ ] Scheduling system enforces 10 hours from **actual** release, not scheduled release.
- [ ] No reduction logic exists anywhere in the system for the ≤14-hour case.
- [ ] Duty periods over 14 hours trigger 12 hours unless the (b)(8) reduced-rest plus ≥14-hour makeup-rest pattern is affirmatively scheduled and tracked.
- [ ] Non-local carrier-provided transportation is excluded from the rest calculation.
- [ ] No duty is assigned during a required rest period.
- [ ] 24 consecutive hours free of all duty within each 7 consecutive calendar days is tracked separately.
- [ ] CBA/manual minimums compared against the regulatory floor; the more restrictive governs.

question: M4
answer:
ANSWER

4 feet (1.2 m) above a lower level — protection is required at 4 feet or more.

Governing provision: 29 CFR 1910.28(b)(1)(i) (OSHA general industry, Walking-Working Surfaces, Subpart D).

1. CONTROLLING REGULATORY TEXT

29 CFR 1910.28(b)(1)(i) — Unprotected sides and edges:

"Except as provided elsewhere in this section, the employer must ensure that each employee on a walking-working surface with an unprotected side or edge that is 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level is protected from falling by one or more of the following:
(A) Guardrail systems;
(B) Safety net systems; or
(C) Personal fall protection systems, such as personal fall arrest, travel restraint, or positioning systems."

Operative reading for the employer:
- Trigger height = 4 ft (1.2 m), measured from the walking-working surface to the lower level.
- The trigger is "4 feet or more." A working surface exactly 4 ft 0 in above the lower level already requires protection; there is no de minimis tolerance in the text.
- The duty is to protect the employee, not merely to post a warning. The three enumerated systems are the baseline means; a warning line or designated area alone does not satisfy (b)(1)(i) for a general walking-working surface.

2. SCOPE / APPLICABILITY DETERMINATION

- Regime: OSHA general industry, 29 CFR Part 1910, Subpart D (Walking-Working Surfaces), section 1910.28 (Duty to have fall protection and falling object protection). This is the correct regime because the question excludes construction (29 CFR Part 1926).
- Rule edition: current text, i.e., the walking-working surfaces rule as revised by the final rule published at 81 FR 82494 (Nov. 18, 2016), effective Jan. 17, 2017 (certain provisions carried later compliance dates, e.g., 1910.30 training and rope descent system provisions). The pre-2017 Subpart D did not contain a single general 4 ft side-and-edge trigger in this form; the 4 ft figure stated here is the current-rule figure and should not be back-applied to pre-2017 conduct without checking the version in force on the relevant date.
- "Walking-working surface" is used in the regulatory sense of 1910.21(b) (any horizontal or vertical surface on or through which an employee walks, works, or gains access to a work area, including floors, roofs, ramps, bridges, runways, formwork, and concrete surfaces, but excluding ladders, vehicles, and trailers used only as a means of access).
- "Unprotected side or edge" = a side or edge without a guardrail system, safety net system, or personal fall protection system complying with 1910.29 / 1910.140.
- The general trigger in (b)(1)(i) is prefaced by "Except as provided elsewhere in this section," so the 4 ft answer is the default that governs any walking-working surface not specifically addressed by another paragraph of 1910.28 or another subpart of Part 1910.

3. CORROBORATION WITHIN THE SAME SECTION (same 4 ft / 1.2 m trigger)

- 1910.28(b)(2)(i) — hoist areas: 4 ft (1.2 m).
- 1910.28(b)(3) — holes: 4 ft (1.2 m) (per the paragraph's stated threshold).
- 1910.28(b)(12)(ii) — rope descent systems: 4 ft (1.2 m).
- 1910.28(b)(14)(i) — slaughtering facility platforms: 4 ft (1.2 m).
- 1910.28(b)(15) — "Walking-working surfaces not otherwise addressed": 4 ft (1.2 m).
The consistency of the 4 ft figure across the section confirms it as the general-industry baseline.

4. THINGS THAT ARE NOT THE ANSWER (guard against mis-citation)

- 6 ft: that is the construction trigger (29 CFR 1926.501(b)(1)) and is expressly outside the question's scope. Do not use it for general industry.
- 6 ft / 15 ft in 1910.28(b)(13): these are distance-from-the-roof-edge triggers for work on low-slope roofs, not height-above-lower-level thresholds. (b)(13) is one of the "elsewhere in this section" provisions that displaces the general (b)(1)(i) trigger for that specific activity, so a low-slope roof question must be analyzed under (b)(13)'s distance bands rather than answered as "4 ft."
- Any state-plan figure: OSHA-approved State Plans must be at least as effective as the federal standard but may differ in specific thresholds and are not addressed by the federal citation above. If the workplace is in a State Plan jurisdiction (e.g., California, Washington, Oregon, Michigan, etc.), verify the state's general-industry fall protection rule before relying on 4 ft.

5. EXCEPTIONS / QUALIFIERS AN EMPLOYER MUST CHECK BEFORE TREATING 4 FT AS DISPOSITIVE

- 1910.28(a)(2) sector carve-outs: the section does not apply to the hazards covered by other cited provisions, including powered platforms (1910.66(j)), aerial lifts (1910.67(c)(2)(v)), telecommunications work (1910.268(n)(7) and (8)), and electric power generation/transmission/distribution (1910.269(g)(2)(i)); the same exclusion list contains additional items preceding (iv) that should be read in full at 1910.28(a)(2) for the specific operation.
- 1910.28(b)(1)(iii) infeasibility exception for the working side of a platform at a loading rack, loading dock, or teeming platform: work may proceed without a fall protection system where the employer can demonstrate a system is not feasible, provided the work operation is in process, access is limited to authorized employees, and those employees are trained per 1910.30.
- 1910.28(b)(1)(ii) residential roofs: where the employer can demonstrate guardrail, safety net, or personal fall protection is infeasible or creates a greater hazard, a written fall protection plan meeting 29 CFR 1926.502(k) plus training meeting 1926.503(a) and (c) is required.
- Comparable infeasibility provisions exist for slaughtering facility platforms (b)(14)(ii).

6. WHAT "PROTECTED" REQUIRES (the obligation that attaches once 4 ft is reached)

- Guardrail systems, safety net systems, or personal fall protection systems selected and installed to 1910.29 (guardrail, safety net, designated area, ladder safety, and warning-line criteria) and, for personal fall protection, 1910.140 (personal fall protection systems).
- Employee training under 1910.30 on the fall hazards present and the procedures/equipment used, plus retraining when workplace changes or employee performance shows it is needed.
- Inspection and maintenance of the fall protection equipment and systems, and prompt repair/replacement of damaged components.
- Note: 1910.28(b)(1)(i) protection is against falls to a lower level; falling-object protection is a separate duty under 1910.28(c) and 1910.29.

7. ONE-LINE ANSWER FOR THE RECORD

Under OSHA general industry rules, an employer must protect an employee on a walking-working surface with an unprotected side or edge from falling when that surface is 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level — 29 CFR 1910.28(b)(1)(i). (Construction, by contrast, is 6 ft under 29 CFR 1926.501(b)(1); that figure does not apply here.)

answer:
# Reserve fuel required for a helicopter beginning a VFR flight in the US

## 1. Answer

**20 minutes.** A helicopter may not begin a VFR flight in the United States unless it carries enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and then, assuming normal cruising speed, to fly for **at least 20 minutes** beyond that point.

The answer is the same under both candidate regulatory bases, so the Part 91 vs. Part 135 ambiguity does not affect the value:

- **Part 91 (private/general operations):** 14 CFR **§91.151(b)** — "No person may begin a flight in a rotorcraft under VFR conditions unless (considering wind and forecast weather conditions) there is enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising speed, to fly after that for at least 20 minutes."
- **Part 135 (commercial/on-demand helicopter operations):** 14 CFR **§135.209(b)** — "No person may begin a flight operation in a helicopter under VFR unless, considering wind and forecast weather conditions, it has enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising fuel consumption, to fly after that for at least 20 minutes."

There is **no day/night difference for helicopters**. The 20-minute reserve applies both day and night. (The 30-minute day / 45-minute night figures exist only in the *airplane* paragraphs, §91.151(a) and §135.209(a).)

## 2. Applicability matrix (who gets which reserve)

| Rule | Operation | Aircraft | Day VFR reserve | Night VFR reserve |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| §91.151(a) | Part 91 | Airplane | 30 min | 45 min |
| **§91.151(b)** | **Part 91** | **Rotorcraft/helicopter** | **20 min** | **20 min** |
| §135.209(a) | Part 135 | Airplane | 30 min | 45 min |
| **§135.209(b)** | **Part 135** | **Helicopter** | **20 min** | **20 min** |

Row highlighted in bold is the answer. A helicopter operator never applies the 30/45-minute airplane figures.

## 3. What the reserve is measured in

The regulation is written in **time**, not distance and not a fixed fuel quantity. The reserve is:

> 20 minutes of flight at **normal cruising speed** (Part 91) / at **normal cruising fuel consumption** (Part 135).

For flight planning it is converted to a fuel quantity using the helicopter's normal cruise fuel flow:

**Reserve fuel (gal) = (20 / 60) × normal cruise fuel flow (gal/hr) = normal cruise fuel flow ÷ 3**

Worked conversions (usable fuel):

| Normal cruise fuel flow | Reserve fuel (20 min) |
|---|---|
| 10 gal/hr | 3.3 gal |
| 12 gal/hr | 4.0 gal |
| 15 gal/hr | 5.0 gal |
| 20 gal/hr | 6.7 gal |
| 30 gal/hr | 10.0 gal |

These are planning conversions, not regulatory thresholds; the only regulatory number is the 20 minutes.

## 4. Procedure to apply the rule to a specific flight

1. **Identify the first point of intended landing.** This is the first airport/helipad/landing site at which the pilot intends to land, as planned before departure. It is not the final destination if an intermediate landing is planned; each leg that begins a new "flight" re-triggers the rule.
2. **Compute trip fuel to that point** using forecast winds and forecast weather conditions (the rule explicitly requires "considering wind and forecast weather conditions"): planned cruise TAS corrected for forecast wind and temperature, plus climb/descent fuel, times the corresponding fuel flows.
3. **Compute the reserve** = 20 minutes × normal cruise fuel flow (Section 3). Use the normal cruise speed/flow the aircraft is actually flown at; do not use a reduced econ-cruise flow to shrink the reserve, because the regulation ties the reserve to *normal* cruising speed/consumption.
4. **Sum:** required fuel at brake release = trip fuel to first point of intended landing + 20-minute reserve. (Any taxi, run-up, and start allowance is a planning add-on, not part of the legal reserve.)
5. **Convert to usable fuel** and confirm it does not exceed usable tank capacity. Fuel listed as **unusable** in the rotorcraft flight manual does not count toward either the trip fuel or the reserve.
6. **Check for anything more restrictive** (Section 5). The 20 minutes is a floor, not a target.
7. **Confirm the aircraft is within limits** — the flight must not require more fuel than the helicopter's maximum fuel capacity/weight-and-balance allows (§91.9(a) — operating within the RFM limitations).

## 5. What the 20 minutes does *not* cover — rules that can raise the minimum

- **Company/operator fuel policy.** Part 135 operators and many Part 91 operators are held to a manual/OpSpecs fuel policy that typically exceeds the regulatory floor. The regulation is a minimum.
- **§91.13 (careless or reckless operation) and §91.3 (PIC authority).** A 20-minute reserve is a legal floor; standard practice and FAA guidance treat a VFR helicopter flight planned to land with only the bare 20 minutes remaining as poor practice, and a pilot is expected to plan conservatively (headwind-adjusted, worst-case burn).
- **RFM/POH limitations** (§91.9(a)) — the aircraft's own fuel and weight limits override any plan.
- **IFR flights are out of scope.** If any portion is flown IFR, a different reserve in §91.167 governs instead; this answer covers VFR only.
- **Public aircraft, military, and foreign-registered operations** are outside this answer; state/local rules and non-US rules are not addressed.

## 6. Common errors this answer is designed to prevent

1. Applying the airplane 30-minute (day) / 45-minute (night) figures to a helicopter — wrong; helicopters are 20 minutes in both cases.
2. Assuming the reserve increases at night for helicopters — it does not.
3. Stating the reserve as a fixed gallon figure or a distance — it is 20 minutes at normal cruising speed, converted to gallons per aircraft type.
4. Applying an IFR alternate-fuel rule to a VFR flight.
5. Counting unusable fuel or fuel that cannot be accessed in flight toward the reserve.
6. Treating the 20 minutes as a planning target rather than a legal minimum.

## 7. Scope and assumptions

- Civil helicopter, US-registered, operating under 14 CFR Part 91 or Part 135, wholly within the United States.
- VFR conditions at departure and as forecast en route.
- The figure given is the **federal regulatory minimum** reserve beyond fuel to the first point of intended landing; operator policy, RFM limits, and good judgment may require more.
- Governing sources: 14 CFR §91.151(b) (Part 91) and §135.209(b) (Part 135), as quoted above.

**Bottom line: 20 minutes of flight at normal cruising speed — day or night, Part 91 or Part 135 — beyond the fuel needed to reach the first point of intended landing.**

1) The RFC that deprecated TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 is RFC 8996, "Deprecating TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1" (March 2021, part of BCP 195; status of the memo: Internet Best Current Practice).

2) The status it gave to the RFCs that had defined those protocol versions — RFC 2246 (TLS 1.0, January 1999) and RFC 4346 (TLS 1.1, April 2006) — is Historic. RFC 8996 moved both documents to Historic status.

- RFC 8996, Section 1 (Introduction): "Transport Layer Security (TLS) versions 1.0 [RFC2246] and 1.1 [RFC4346] were superseded by TLS 1.2 [RFC5246] in 2008, which has now itself been superseded by TLS 1.3 [RFC8446]. ... Therefore, it is timely to further deprecate TLS 1.0, TLS 1.1, and DTLS 1.0. Accordingly, the aforementioned documents have been moved to Historic status."
- RFC Editor info page for RFC 2246 shows status "Historic" (https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc2246).

- Datatracker history for RFC 8996 records the RFC Editor sync with title "Deprecating TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1" and the same abstract wording (https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc8996/history/).

DOCUMENT / STATUS LEDGER (so the two values are not conflated)

| Document | Role | Status assigned by RFC 8996 |
|---|---|---|
| RFC 8996 | The deprecating document (BCP 195) | Internet Best Current Practice (its own memo status) |
| RFC 2246 | Defines TLS 1.0 | Historic |
| RFC 4346 | Defines TLS 1.1 | Historic |
| RFC 4347 | Defines DTLS 1.0 (deprecated by the same RFC, but not a TLS 1.0/1.1 defining document) | Historic |
| RFC 5469 | DES/IDEA cipher suites, only usable with now-Historic versions | Historic |
| RFC 5246 (TLS 1.2) | Not deprecated by RFC 8996 | Remains Standards Track (superseded in practice by TLS 1.3, RFC 8446) |

PRECISION NOTES

- "Historic" is the status value. Do not confuse it with the separate obsoletion relationship shown on the RFC Editor pages ("This RFC is now obsolete, see RFC 4346" for RFC 2246; "...see RFC 5246" for RFC 4346). Obsoleted-by is a document relationship; Historic is the stream status that RFC 8996 applied. The question asks for the status, so the answer is Historic.
- RFC 8996 is not Standards Track; its own Status of This Memo reads "This memo documents an Internet Best Current Practice," and it updates RFC 7525, making it part of BCP 195.
- The deprecation is normative for IETF usage: TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 implementations are to be avoided, and the RFC also forbids negotiation of DTLS 1.0 (updating RFC 6347).
- Scope: this answer covers the IETF RFC Series only. Stances of other standards bodies on TLS 1.0/1.1 are out of scope for both asks.

**The 2026 US Social Security contribution and benefit base (the OASDI taxable maximum) is $184,500.**

That is the maximum amount of an individual's 2026 annual earnings — wages, other covered compensation, and net self-employment income — subject to the Social Security (OASDI) payroll tax, and simultaneously the maximum amount of 2026 earnings creditable in a Social Security benefit computation.

This is an official, published determination, not a projection. It was set by the Commissioner of Social Security under the automatic-indexing formula in the Social Security Act and announced with the 2026 COLA package.

---

## 1. Authority and corroboration

| Source | What it states for 2026 |
|---|---|
| SSA, Office of the Chief Actuary — *Contribution and Benefit Base* (ssa.gov/oact/COLA/cbb.html) | History table: 2024 $168,600; 2025 $176,100; **2026 $184,500**; 2027 $192,300. Defines the figure as the annual limit on earnings subject to OASDI taxation and usable in benefit computations ("taxable maximum"). |
| SSA — *Automatic Determinations in Recent Years* (ssa.gov/oact/COLA/autoAdj.html) | 2026 row: COLA 3.6%; contribution and benefit base **$184,500**; retirement earnings test exempt amounts $24,480 (lower) / $65,160 (higher). |
| SSA — *EFW2 Tax Year 2026*, Pub. No. 42-007 (ssa.gov/employer/efw/26efw2.pdf, dated 11/12/2026) | "The Social Security Wage Base for tax year 2026 is $184,500." Social Security wages/tips "should not exceed the annual maximum Social Security wage base for the tax year ($184,500 for tax year 2026)"; Social Security tax withheld "should not exceed $11,439.00 for tax year 2026." |
| Congressional Research Service, IF11747 (current version) | "the Social Security payroll tax is applied to covered earnings up to an annual limit, or taxable maximum ($184,500 in 2026)" — and identifies this as both the contribution base and the benefit base. |

Four independent official/authoritative sources agree on $184,500, and the SSA employer-instruction document independently confirms the derived withholding cap of $11,439.00.

---

## 2. Independent derivation from the statutory formula (verification, not source of the answer)

Under the Social Security Act as amended, the base for year Y after 1994 is:

    Base(Y) = $60,600 x [ AWI(Y-2) / AWI(1992) ] , rounded to the nearest multiple of $300

(never reduced below the prior year's base). The formula applies only in years for which a December COLA is effective; a COLA is effective for December 2026, so the determination was properly made.

Inputs and computation for Y = 2026 (using AWI for 2024, i.e. Y-2):

- 1994 base = $60,600
- AWI(1992) = $22,935.42
- AWI(2024) = $69,846.57

    ratio = 69,846.57 / 22,935.42 = 3.045358...
    unrounded base = 60,600 x 3.045358 = $184,548.7
    round to nearest $300 -> $184,500

Rounding check: $184,548.7 is $48.70 above $184,500 and $251.30 below $184,800, so the nearest multiple of $300 is $184,500. The result exceeds the 2025 base of $176,100, so the no-reduction rule does not bind.

Same-method control on the adjacent year, to prove the table is being read correctly: for 2027, 60,600 x (72,800.33 / 22,935.42) = $192,353.14 -> $192,300, which is exactly the figure SSA publishes for 2027.

---

## 3. Derived payroll figures for 2026 (internal consistency checks)

| Item | 2026 value | Derivation |
|---|---|---|
| Contribution and benefit base (OASDI taxable maximum) | **$184,500** | Official determination |
| Employee OASDI rate | 6.2% | Statute (unchanged) |
| Employer OASDI rate | 6.2% | Statute (unchanged) |
| Combined OASDI rate | 12.4% | 6.2% + 6.2% |
| Maximum OASDI tax — employee | **$11,439.00** | 0.062 x 184,500 |
| Maximum OASDI tax — employer | **$11,439.00** | 0.062 x 184,500 |
| Maximum combined employee + employer | **$22,878.00** | 0.124 x 184,500 |
| Self-employment OASDI tax rate | 12.4% | Statute |
| Maximum OASDI tax — self-employed | **$22,878.00** | 0.124 x 184,500 |

The $11,439.00 figure reproduces the SSA EFW2 Tax Year 2026 hard cap exactly ("should not exceed $11,439.00 for tax year 2026"), which is an independent confirmation that $184,500 is the operative base rather than a stale or projected value.

---

## 4. Scope boundaries — what $184,500 does and does not cap

- **Applies to:** OASDI (Old-Age, Survivors, and Disability Insurance) only — wages, tips reported as Social Security tips, and net self-employment income. The same $184,500 applies both to the contribution side (taxation) and the benefit side (earnings creditable in the AIME/benefit formula).
- **Does NOT apply to:** Medicare Hospital Insurance (HI). There has been no HI taxable maximum since 1993; all 2026 Medicare wages are taxable, with the additional 0.9% HI surtax above statutory thresholds ($200,000 single / $250,000 joint) unaffected by this base.
- **Not the same as:** the retirement earnings test exempt amounts ($24,480 lower / $65,160 higher for 2026), the quarters-of-coverage threshold, the PIA bend points ($1,286 / $7,749 for 2026), or the "old-law" base used for Railroad Retirement/ERISA purposes (reported by SSA as $137,100 for 2026). None of these is the payroll-tax base; do not substitute them.
- **Jurisdiction:** US federal only. State unemployment/disability wage bases are separate and unrelated.

---

## 5. Caveats and confidence

- **Confidence: high.** The figure is an official SSA determination, published in SSA's own current-year employer instructions, corroborated by CRS, and reproducible from the statutory formula to the dollar before rounding.
- **Legislative risk:** the value is set under current law and would change only if Congress amended the indexing formula or the 1994 base before/within tax year 2026. No such intervening change is reflected in the sources consulted; the SSA employer instruction dated 11/12/2026 (i.e., current for tax year 2026) still states $184,500.
- **Column-alignment note:** the "old-law" base and quarters-of-coverage figures above are read from a table whose full column headers were only partially captured in the retrieved text; treat those two secondary numbers as informational. They do not affect the answer, which rests on the explicit prose statements in the SSA base page and the EFW2 publication.

---

## 6. One-line answer for downstream use

> 2026 Social Security contribution and benefit base = **$184,500** (maximum OASDI-taxable earnings; maximum employee tax $11,439.00 at 6.2%; maximum self-employment OASDI tax $22,878.00 at 12.4%; Medicare wages uncapped).
