CURRENT U.S. BASICMED AIRCRAFT LIMITS (post-FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024)

| Limit | Current BasicMed limit |
|---|---|
| Maximum takeoff weight | 12,500 lb maximum certificated takeoff weight |
| Maximum occupants the aircraft may be authorized to carry | 7 occupants, including any required flightcrew members |
| Maximum passengers on board | 6 passengers |

1. MAXIMUM TAKEOFF WEIGHT: 12,500 lb.
The aircraft must have a maximum certificated takeoff weight of not more than 12,500 pounds. For experimental aircraft, which are not type certificated, the relevant maximum takeoff weight is the maximum takeoff weight established for the aircraft rather than a type-certificate maximum. The 2024 final rule uses 'maximum takeoff weight' for this reason.

2. OCCUPANTS THE AIRCRAFT MAY BE AUTHORIZED TO CARRY: 7 occupants.
The aircraft must be authorized under Federal law to carry not more than 7 occupants. This is the aircraft's authorized occupancy limit, not merely the number of seats currently installed. For type-certificated aircraft, the relevant authorization is the aircraft's design approval (type certificate, supplemental type certificate, or amended type certificate). An aircraft authorized for 8 or more occupants does not qualify even if fewer seats are installed. The 7-occupant count includes required flightcrew members and the pilot operating under BasicMed.

3. PASSENGERS ON BOARD: 6 passengers.
The operation may carry not more than 6 passengers. With one pilot operating under BasicMed, that yields 7 total occupants: 1 pilot + 6 passengers. If the aircraft is type certificated for, or the regulations require, more than one pilot flightcrew member, the 7-occupant cap controls: for example, 2 required flightcrew members + 5 passengers = 7 occupants, so the sixth passenger cannot be carried even though the passenger limit itself is 6. The regulatory maximum passenger limit is therefore 6; the achievable passenger count may be lower when additional required flightcrew are aboard.

SCOPE AND EXCLUSIONS
- This applies to a pilot eligible for and operating under BasicMed, not to operations requiring an FAA medical certificate.
- The aircraft must not be a transport-category rotorcraft certificated to airworthiness standards under 14 CFR part 29. The 2024 expansion expressly excludes those rotorcraft.
- Other BasicMed operating limits remain: within the United States, at or below 18,000 feet MSL, at an indicated airspeed of 250 knots or less, and not for compensation or hire.

SOURCES
- FAA, BasicMed (current webpage), Aircraft Requirements and Operating Requirements: 'Any aircraft authorized under federal law to carry not more than 7 occupants'; 'Has a maximum certificated takeoff weight of not more than 12,500 pounds'; 'Carries not more than six passengers.' https://www.faa.gov/licenses_certificates/airmen_certification/basic_med
- FAA, 'FAA Updates BasicMed Program' (Nov. 15, 2024): increases passengers to six from five, occupants to seven from six, and maximum takeoff weight to 12,500 lb from 6,000 lb, excluding transport category helicopters. https://www.faa.gov/newsroom/faa-updates-basicmed-program
- FAA final rule, document 2024-26935 (Nov. 18, 2024): 49 U.S.C. 44703 note / FESSA §2307(j), as amended by FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024 §828(a)(4); 14 CFR 61.113(i)(1); 14 CFR 91.319(j). The final rule states a covered aircraft 'may now be authorized to carry up to 7 occupants (including any required flight crewmembers) and may be operating with up to 6 passengers on board.' https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2024-11-18/html/2024-26935.htm
- AC 68-1A (2017) and AC 68-1 (2017) state the older 6,000 lb / 6-occupant / 5-passenger limits. Those ACs predate the 2024 statutory amendment and implementing final rule and are superseded on these three numeric limits by the current rule and FAA BasicMed page.

HISTORICAL NOTE
Before the 2024 expansion, the limits were 6,000 lb maximum certificated takeoff weight, 6 occupants, and 5 passengers. Those are not the current limits.

answer:
US FEDERAL HOURS-OF-SERVICE LIMITS — DRIVERS OF PASSENGER-CARRYING COMMERCIAL MOTOR VEHICLES (MOTORCOACH)

Governing authority: 49 CFR 395.5 (Maximum driving time for passenger-carrying vehicles), subject to the exceptions and exemptions in 49 CFR 395.1. Definitions in 49 CFR 395.2. This is the rule set for interstate operation of a passenger-carrying CMV (designed/used to transport 9 or more passengers including the driver, per 49 CFR 390.5) — for-hire or private — and it is distinct from the property-carrying rule set in 49 CFR 395.3.

=== THE THREE ANSWERS ===

1) HOW MANY HOURS MAY THEY DRIVE: 10 hours.
   49 CFR 395.5(a)(1): no carrier may permit or require, and no driver may drive, a passenger-carrying CMV "[m]ore than 10 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty."

2) AFTER HOW MANY CONSECUTIVE HOURS OFF DUTY: 8 consecutive hours.
   The 8-consecutive-hour off-duty period is the precondition and reset built into both 395.5(a)(1) and (a)(2): the 10-hour driving allowance and the 15-hour on-duty allowance each run "following 8 consecutive hours off duty." A driver may not lawfully begin a new driving period until 8 consecutive hours off duty have been taken.

3) AFTER HOW MANY HOURS ON DUTY MAY THEY NO LONGER DRIVE: 15 hours on duty.
   49 CFR 395.5(a)(2): no carrier may permit or require, and no driver may drive, "[f]or any period after having been on duty 15 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty."

Summary table (49 CFR 395.5):

| Limit | Passenger-carrying CMV (this answer) | Citation |
|---|---|---|
| Maximum driving time | 10 hours | 395.5(a)(1) |
| Off-duty reset required before driving | 8 consecutive hours | 395.5(a)(1), (a)(2) |
| On-duty threshold after which driving is prohibited | 15 hours | 395.5(a)(2) |
| Weekly on-duty cap (carrier not operating every day) | 60 hours in 7 consecutive days | 395.5(b)(1) |
| Weekly on-duty cap (carrier operating every day) | 70 hours in 8 consecutive days | 395.5(b)(2) |

=== HOW THE THREE LIMITS INTERACT (the part that gets violated in practice) ===

- The 15-hour figure is an ON-DUTY clock, not a 14-hour "driving window" and not a driving cap. It starts when the driver begins work or is required to be in readiness for work, and it runs continuously through driving time, on-duty-not-driving time (loading, inspections, paperwork, waiting to be dispatched), and any compensated work for a non-motor-carrier. Driving must stop at the 15th hour even if the driver has driven far fewer than 10 hours. Example: on duty at 06:00, only 6 hours of actual driving completed by 20:30 — driving must still cease at 21:00.
- The 10-hour cap and the 15-hour cap are independent ceilings. Whichever is reached first ends driving. Example: on duty 06:00, driving 06:00-16:00 = 10 hours driven, which ends driving at 16:00 (the 10-hour cap binds first); the driver is nonetheless still within the 15-hour on-duty limit until 21:00 but may not drive.
- The 8-consecutive-hour off-duty period resets the 10-hour and 15-hour clocks. It does NOT reset the 60/70-hour weekly clock — see below.
- Off-duty status for meal and routine stops requires that the driver be relieved of all duty and responsibility for the care and custody of the bus/CMV, its accessories, and any passengers, baggage and freight being transported (FMCSA, Hours of Service for Motor Carriers of Passengers). A driver who remains responsible for the vehicle or passengers is not off duty, and such time counts against the 15-hour on-duty allowance.
- "On-duty time" (49 CFR 395.2) is all time from the time the driver begins work or is required to be in readiness for work until relieved from work and all responsibility for performing work; it includes driving, all other work for the carrier, waiting to be dispatched, and compensated work for a person who is not a motor carrier. "Off-duty time" is not separately defined; in effect it is any time that is not driving time, on-duty time, or sleeper-berth time. When a driver works more than one job of any kind, that time is also on-duty time.
- Multiple-employer drivers: the 10-hour and 15-hour limits apply regardless of the number of motor carriers using the driver's services (395.5(b)); the carrier must obtain a signed statement of total on-duty time for the preceding 7 days and the time the driver was last relieved from duty (49 CFR 395.8(j)).

=== WEEKLY LIMITS (companion limits; not a substitute for the three answers) ===

49 CFR 395.5(b): a driver may not drive after having been on duty —
(1) 60 hours in any 7 consecutive days, if the employing carrier does not operate CMVs every day of the week; or
(2) 70 hours in any period of 8 consecutive days, if the employing carrier operates CMVs every day of the week.
The 8-hour off-duty reset does not clear these; only a qualifying 34-hour-plus off-duty period would, and the 34-hour restart provision (49 CFR 395.3(c)) sits in the property-carrying section and is therefore not available to passenger-carrying drivers. "7 or 8 consecutive days" means the 7 or 8 consecutive 24-hour periods designated by the carrier for the driver's home terminal (49 CFR 395.8(a)(8)(ii)).

=== WHAT DOES NOT APPLY TO PASSENGER-CARRYING DRIVERS ===

State these only as contrasts; they are not the answer for a motorcoach:
- 11-hour driving limit, 14-hour driving window, 10-consecutive-hour off-duty reset, 30-minute break after 8 cumulative hours, and 34-hour restart are PROPERTY-CARRYING limits under 49 CFR 395.3 and do not apply here. A passenger-carrying driver is not required to take the 30-minute break and is not permitted to use the 34-hour restart.
- The short-haul exception in 49 CFR 395.1(e) is written for property-carrying CMVs; it does not reduce the 10/8/15 figures above for a passenger carrier.

=== EXCEPTIONS THAT CAN CHANGE THE NUMBERS (verify applicability before relying on them) ===

- Sleeper berth, passenger-carrying: a driver of a passenger-carrying CMV equipped with a sleeper berth (49 CFR 393.76) may accumulate the equivalent of 8 consecutive hours off duty by taking two periods of rest in the sleeper berth, provided the four requirements of 49 CFR 395.1(g)(3)(i)-(iv) are met. Confirm the four conditions against the regulation text before applying; absent compliance with all four, the full 8 consecutive hours off duty is required.
- Adverse driving conditions / emergency: 49 CFR 395.1(b) provides an exception that can extend driving time. The 2020 amendments' fixed 2-hour extension was written for the property-carrying limits in 395.3; confirm the operative text of 395.1(b) for the passenger-carrying application rather than assuming the property-carrying extension applies.
- Alaska: 49 CFR 395.1(h) sets a separate passenger-carrying variant for operation in Alaska — driving not more than 15 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty, no driving after being on duty 20 hours or more following 8 consecutive hours off duty, and 70 hours in 7 days / 80 hours in 8 days. This applies only to operation in Alaska; it does not alter the 10/8/15 figures for the rest of the United States.
- Carrier-specific exemptions, state intrastate rules, and any FMCSA emergency declarations/waivers in effect on the date of use must be checked separately; this answer states the general federal interstate rule.

=== RECORDKEEPING / ENFORCEMENT CONTEXT ===

- Record of duty status: 49 CFR 395.8. ELD regulations apply to most motor carriers of passengers and their drivers required to keep a RODS; a listed exception is drivers required to prepare a RODS no more than 8 days in any 30-day period. Records and supporting documents must be retained at least 6 months.
- Drivers declared out of service: 49 CFR 395.13.

=== CITATIONS ===
49 CFR 395.5(a)(1), (a)(2), (b)(1), (b)(2) (primary; eCFR and 2021 CFR print agree, [70 FR 50073, Aug. 25, 2005]); 49 CFR 395.1 (exceptions, incl. (b), (g)(3), (h), (j)); 49 CFR 395.2 (definitions); 49 CFR 395.8 (RODS; (a)(8), (j)); 49 CFR 390.5 (CMV definition); FMCSA, "Hours of Service for Motor Carriers of Passengers"; FMCSA Safety Planner 6.4.3 "Passenger-Carrying Operations (395.5)."

Scope note: this answer is the federal interstate rule for passenger-carrying CMVs (motorcoach-type operation) as of the date of use. If the driver operates solely intrastate, or under a state variant, or under an active emergency waiver, the numbers must be re-confirmed against that authority.

Regulatory basis: 14 CFR §135.273, 'Duty period limitations and rest requirements: Flight attendants.' Section 135.261(e) states that §135.273 prescribes duty period limitations and rest requirements for flight attendants in all operations conducted under Part 135, which includes on-demand charter operations. 'Rest period' is defined in §135.273(a) as 'the period free of all responsibility for work or duty should the occasion arise.'

ASK 1 — Rest after a scheduled duty period of 14 hours or less: 9 consecutive hours.
Section 135.273(b)(2) provides: 'Except as provided in paragraph (b)(3) of this section, a flight attendant scheduled to a duty period of 14 hours or less as provided under paragraph (b)(1) of this section must be given a scheduled rest period of at least 9 consecutive hours. This rest period must occur between the completion of the scheduled duty period and the commencement of the subsequent duty period.'

ASK 2 — Reduction floor: 8 consecutive hours, conditional.
Section 135.273(b)(3) permits the 9-hour rest to be 'scheduled for or reduced to a minimum of 8 hours if the flight attendant is given a subsequent rest period of at least 10 consecutive hours; this subsequent rest period must be scheduled to begin no later than 24 hours after the beginning of the reduced rest period and must occur between the completion of the scheduled duty period and the commencement of the subsequent duty period.'
Thus the rest may be reduced to no less than 8 consecutive hours, and only if the operator also provides the required subsequent rest of at least 10 consecutive hours beginning within 24 hours after the start of the reduced rest. If those conditions are not met, the rest cannot be reduced below 9 consecutive hours.

Related limits:
- Section 135.273(b)(10) prohibits assigning a flight attendant to any duty period unless the flight attendant has had at least the minimum rest required by §135.273.
- Section 135.273(b)(11) prohibits assigning a flight attendant to perform any duty during a required rest period.
- The separate reduced-rest provision in §135.273(b)(8), which allows rest to be reduced to 10 consecutive hours with a 14-hour subsequent rest, applies to the rest required under §135.273(b)(7). It is not the reduction authority for the 9-hour rest required under §135.273(b)(2) after a scheduled duty period of 14 hours or less.

Caveats:
- If the certificate holder has elected the §135.273(c) alternative to apply flight crewmember duty/rest rules to flight attendants, the answer must be determined under the Administrator-approved written procedures and operations specifications; this answer assumes no such election.
- If the actual duty period exceeds the scheduled duty period by more than one hour, §135.273(b)(7) through (b)(9) may impose additional rest requirements.
- Operator manuals, operations specifications, or collective bargaining agreements may impose rest greater than the regulatory minimum; the values above are the regulatory minimum.

Bottom line: After a scheduled duty period of 14 hours or less, a Part 135 flight attendant must receive at least 9 consecutive hours of rest. That rest may be reduced to no less than 8 consecutive hours only if the flight attendant is given a subsequent rest period of at least 10 consecutive hours beginning no later than 24 hours after the beginning of the reduced rest period.

# HTTP/2: current specification and its obsoletes

## 1. Answer

| Ask | Answer |
|---|---|
| Current specification of HTTP/2 | **RFC 9113**, *HTTP/2*, June 2022, M. Thomson & C. Benfield (Eds.), Standards Track / Proposed Standard |
| RFCs it obsoletes | **RFC 7540** and **RFC 8740** (two documents, direct obsoletes relationship) |

Short form: **RFC 9113 is the current HTTP/2 specification; it obsoletes RFC 7540 and RFC 8740.**

## 2. Evidence

### 2.1 RFC 9113 is the current specification

RFC Editor info page (https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9113/):

> "RFC 9113: HTTP/2 — HTTP/2 — June 2022. M. Thomson, Ed., C. Benfield, Ed. — Proposed Standard"
>
> "This specification describes an optimized expression of the semantics of the Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP), referred to as HTTP version 2 (HTTP/2). HTTP/2 enables a more efficient use of network resources and a reduced latency by introducing field compression and allowing multiple concurrent exchanges on the same connection."

RFC Editor subject page for HTTP/2 (https://www.rfc-editor.org/subjects/http2/) lists RFC 9113 first in the set and marks the predecessor:

> RFC 7540 … "Obsoleted by RFC 9113"

Datatracker (https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9113) corroborates the same document and status:

> "Document type: RFC — Proposed Standard, June 2022"

No obsoleting successor to RFC 9113 is recorded on either the RFC Editor info page or the Datatracker entry as of the source-fetch date (2026-11-16). RFC 9113 is therefore the RFC in force for HTTP/2.

### 2.2 What RFC 9113 obsoletes

From the RFC 9113 document header itself (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/inline-errata/rfc9113.html, and mirrored on Datatracker):

> "Request for Comments: 9113 … Obsoletes: 7540, 8740 … Category: Standards Track … June 2022"

And in the abstract:

> "This document obsoletes RFCs 7540 and 8740."

Datatracker restates it in metadata form:

> "Obsoletes RFC 8740, RFC 7540"

So the obsoletes set is exactly:

| Obsoleted RFC | What it was |
|---|---|
| **RFC 7540** | *Hypertext Transfer Protocol Version 2 (HTTP/2)*, May 2015 — the original HTTP/2 specification. Source pages mark it "Obsoleted by RFC 9113". |
| **RFC 8740** | The HTTP/2-over-TLS-1.3 document, which had itself *updated* RFC 7540. RFC 9113 folds its content in: "Use of TLS 1.3 was defined based on [RFC8740], which this document obsoletes" (Appendix B). The RFC Editor subject page marks it "Obsoleted by RFC 9113". |

*(RFC 8740's full title and authorship are not load-bearing for this answer and are not asserted here as verified; the fetched passages establish only its subject matter and its obsoleted status. Its commonly cited title is "Using TLS 1.3 with HTTP/2" — treat that as supplementary.)*

## 3. Conventions used (so the answer is not over-read)

1. **"Current"** = the RFC in force at the time of answering, per the RFC Editor and IETF Datatracker records, not a historical revision and not a project-pinned date.
2. **"Obsoletes"** = the direct `Obsoletes:` relationship declared in RFC 9113's own header/abstract. This is the narrow, authoritative reading. The transitive chain adds nothing here: RFC 9113's header lists 7540 and 8740, and 8740's only predecessor link (7540) is already in that list.
3. **Status wording** — RFC 9113 is labelled *Proposed Standard* by the RFC Editor and carries category *Standards Track* in its header. Both labels are reported as found; neither is upgraded to "Internet Standard" in this answer.
4. **Extensions are out of scope for the obsoletes list.** HTTP/2 has separate extension/update RFCs — e.g. RFC 8441 (Bootstrapping WebSockets with HTTP/2) and RFC 8336 (The ORIGIN HTTP/2 Frame), both visible on the same subject page — that *extend* HTTP/2 and are **not** obsoleted by RFC 9113. "Updates" ≠ "Obsoletes": an RFC that updates another remains in force unless it is itself obsoleted or its content is folded in, which is exactly what happened to 8740 and not to 8441/8336.
5. **Errata** do not change which RFC is the current specification. RFC 9113 has an inline-errata rendering at https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/inline-errata/rfc9113.html; the errata ledger state was not read in the source passages, so no claim about the presence or count of verified errata is made here.

## 4. Re-verification procedure (≈60 seconds, authoritative sources only)

1. Open `https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9113/`. Confirm the title is *HTTP/2*, that the page carries no "Obsoleted by" banner, and note the `Obsoletes:` line.
2. Open `https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9113` and confirm the metadata block reads `Obsoletes RFC 8740, RFC 7540` and that no successor document is listed.
3. Open `https://www.rfc-editor.org/subjects/http2/` and confirm the newest entry in the HTTP/2 set is RFC 9113, with RFC 7540 and RFC 8740 both annotated "Obsoleted by RFC 9113".
4. Do **not** substitute secondary sources (vendor docs, Wikipedia, MDN) for steps 1–3; they are the usual origin of stale "RFC 7540" answers.

If step 1 or step 3 ever shows a document that obsoletes RFC 9113, that document becomes the answer to ask 1 and its own `Obsoletes:` line becomes the answer to ask 2.

## 5. One-line citable statement

> The current specification of HTTP/2 is RFC 9113 (*HTTP/2*, June 2022, Standards Track/Proposed Standard, Thomson & Benfield, Eds.). Per its header and abstract, it obsoletes RFC 7540 (the original HTTP/2 specification, 2015) and RFC 8740 (the TLS 1.3 update to HTTP/2).

Scope: U.S. federal FMCSA hours-of-service rules, 49 CFR Part 395, current regulatory text, specifically the general property-carrying short-haul exception in 49 CFR 395.1(e)(1).

1. Radius: The driver must operate within a 150 air-mile radius of the normal work reporting location. The regulation states this as "150 air-mile radius (172.6 statute miles)." The controlling unit is air miles, i.e., straight-line distance, not 150 road/statute miles; 172.6 statute miles is the parenthetical approximate conversion in the regulatory text.

2. Release from work: The driver must return to the work reporting location and be released from work within 14 consecutive hours. The 14-hour period runs consecutively from the time the driver comes on duty; the driver must both return to the normal work reporting location and be released from work within that 14-consecutive-hour window.

Regulatory basis, 49 CFR 395.1(e)(1): A driver is exempt from the requirements of 49 CFR 395.8 and 395.11 if, among other conditions, the driver operates within a 150 air-mile radius of the normal work reporting location and, except a driver-salesperson, returns to the work reporting location and is released from work within 14 consecutive hours. The same provision also requires at least 10 consecutive hours off duty separating each 14 hours on duty for a property-carrying CMV driver, and requires the employing motor carrier to maintain and retain accurate time records for 6 months showing report-for-duty time, total on-duty hours each day, release-from-duty time, and the preceding 7 days' total time for certain newly used or intermittent drivers.

Compliance note: If the driver exceeds the 150 air-mile radius or is not returned and released within 14 consecutive hours, the short-haul exception is not satisfied for that day, and the driver must complete a record of duty status for that day as required. The exception does not eliminate the 11-hour driving limit or other applicable hours-of-service limits; it relieves the driver of the RODS and supporting-documents requirements only when all of its conditions are met.

question: H1
answer:
## Answer

**10 consecutive hours.** For a US air carrier operating under Part 121 (domestic, flag or supplemental operations), the federal minimum rest period between a flight attendant’s duty periods is **10 consecutive hours**, and it **may not be reduced** — not by the carrier, not by scheduling, not because of a delay.

Authority: 14 CFR §121.467(b)(2) and (b)(3).

> (b)(2) “A flight attendant scheduled to a duty period of 14 hours or less as provided under paragraph (b)(1) of this section must be given a scheduled rest period of at least 10 consecutive hours. This rest period must occur between the completion of the scheduled duty period and the commencement of the subsequent duty period.”
>
> (b)(3) “The rest period required under paragraph (b)(2) of this section may not be reduced to less than 10 consecutive hours.”

This is a **floor**, not a target. A carrier may give more (and frequently must, under its CBA — see below), but never less.

## Scope conditions that change the number

- **Part 121 scheduled/charter (the assumed case):** 10 hours, non-reducible.
- **Part 135 / §91.1062 (program manager, on-demand charter):** the figure is **9 consecutive hours**, and §91.1062(a)(3) permits scheduling/reducing it to 8 hours if a compensating 10-hour rest is given within 24 hours. That is a different regime and does **not** answer “US airline” in the ordinary sense.
- **Carrier election under §121.467(c):** a certificate holder may, by written procedures, apply the Part 117 flightcrew-member duty/rest scheme to its flight attendants instead. If — and only if — the carrier has made that election, the Part 117 rest scheme governs and the 10-hour figure must be re-derived from Part 117. Confirm from the carrier’s operations manual whether the (c) election is in effect.
- **Extended-duty assignments under §121.467(b)(4)–(b)(6):** the 10-hour figure above is tied to duty periods of 14 hours or less. Assignments made under the extended-duty exceptions carry their own rest conditions in those subparagraphs, which can be longer. Read the current subparagraph text before relying on 10:00 for an extended-duty pairing.

## How to compute the rest window (procedure)

1. **Start** = release from the prior duty period (the end of the duty period as defined in §121.467(a): elapsed time from report for an assignment involving flight time to release from that assignment).
2. **End** = report time for the next duty period — i.e., the start of duty, including any carrier-required pre-flight briefing, security, or check-in. Report time, not block-out, closes the window.
3. **Rest = (next report) − (prior release)**, computed as elapsed time. The regulation’s definitions permit calculation in local time or UTC, but it must reflect total elapsed time; crossing time zones does not create or destroy rest hours. Ten hours is ten elapsed hours.
4. **Test:** rest ≥ 10:00 (600 minutes). Anything under 600 minutes is a hard fail with no operational override.
5. **Worked example:** release at 21:35 → earliest lawful report is 07:35 the following day. A 06:00 report on that pairing is unlawful regardless of how the 21:35 release came about.

## What the 10 hours must be free of

§121.467(a) defines a rest period as “the period free of all restraint or duty … and free of all responsibility for work or duty should the occasion arise.” Compliance consequences:

- The window must be **scheduled** into the pairing (b)(2) says “scheduled rest period” — it is not enough that the gap happens to occur.
- Carrier-imposed obligations during the window (required calls, mandatory training, positioning, being held on call) are restraint/responsibility and must be assessed as eating into or eliminating rest. Positioning flown for the carrier is duty, not rest.
- **Delays do not shrink rest.** The FAA’s interpretation of §121.467 (the “Fell” letter) is explicit: circumstances beyond the carrier’s control permit exceeding duty-period limitations under (b)(14), but “does not permit reducing required rest periods.” If a mechanical or weather delay pushes release late, the carrier must push the next report correspondingly or remove the assignment. The delay is not a credit against the rest floor.
- **Mid-duty rest is a separate question.** §121.467 sets rest between duty periods; it does not establish a federal minimum for breaks within a duty period. Mid-duty breaks come from the CBA or carrier policy and should not be counted toward the 10-hour figure.

## Where a higher number may govern

Collective bargaining agreements routinely exceed the federal floor, and where they do, the CBA is the operative minimum for that carrier. Example (Frontier flight attendant agreement, REST PERIOD, §C):

- In base: no less than **11:00 scheduled**, **10:00 actual**.
- Reserve returning to base after a red-eye: **12:00**.
- Out of base: not scheduled for or given less than **10:00**.
- Scaled to actual duty: under 16:00 duty → **10:00**; 16:00–17:00 duty → **13:00**; over 17:00 duty → **15:00**.

Every one of those is at or above the federal 10:00, which is exactly the relationship to expect: the CBA can raise the floor, never lower it. Carriers also impose their own policy minimums (often 10:00–12:00) and fatigue-risk-management limits; those are binding on the carrier as a matter of policy and of its FAA-approved procedures even where the regulation is silent.

## Trap: the 9-hour figure still in circulation

Older FAA guidance and legal-interpretation documents quote §121.467(b)(2) as “at least 9 consecutive hours.” That is the **pre-amendment** text. The current eCFR text of §121.467(b)(2)–(3) reads 10 hours and expressly bars reduction. If a scheduler, manual, or third-party summary cites 9 hours for a Part 121 carrier, it is out of date. Verify the section against the eCFR as of the date of applicability before relying on it; the 9-hour figure should be used only for the Part 135 / §91.1062 regime, where it is correct.

## Auditor’s checklist

1. Confirm the carrier’s operating regime (Part 121 vs. Part 135) and whether the §121.467(c) Part 117 election is in effect.
2. Pull the applicable CBA rest article and the carrier’s manual rest provision; take the **highest** of regulation, CBA, and policy.
3. For every pairing, compute release→report in elapsed minutes; flag every result under 600 minutes (or under the CBA figure, if higher) as a hard fail.
4. Confirm the rest is scheduled in the pairing, not merely achieved by chance.
5. Confirm no carrier-imposed duty or responsibility sits inside the window.
6. On irregular operations, confirm that any (b)(14) duty extension was accompanied by a corresponding push of the next report — never by a shortened rest.
7. Retain the pairing records and the rest computation; that is the evidence of compliance.

The first reads: "(2) A flight attendant scheduled to a duty period of 14 hours or less as provided under paragraph (b)(1) of this section must be given a scheduled rest period of at least 10 consecutive hours."
